passages.original: MARCION quoque, a quo Marcionitæ appellati sunt I, Cerdonis secutus est dogmata de duobus principiis : quamvis Epiphanius eum tria dicat asseruisse principia, bonum, justum, pravum : sed Eusebius Sinerum quemdam , non Marcionem, trium principiorum atque naturarum scribit auctorem (Euseb. lib. 5, cap. 13).
passages.english: Marcion too, from whom the Marcionites are named, followed the teachings of Cerdo on two first principles; although Epiphanius says that he asserted three principles, good, just, and evil. But Eusebius writes that a certain Sinerus, not Marcion, was the author of [the doctrine of] three principles and natures (Eusebius, book 5, chapter 13).
passages.notes: The stray "I" after "appellati sunt" is taken as a footnote mark and omitted. "Sinerum" is given as printed (Sinerus). The name is uncertain, possibly a corruption of another name in Eusebius.

passages.original: XLII. ORIGENIANI a quodam Origene dicti sunt; non illo qui rere omnibus notus est, sed ab alio ne- scio quo, de quo vel sectatoribus ejus Epiphanius toquens : Origeniani, inquit, cujusdam Origenis 2; turpis autem sunt operationis, isti sunt nefanda facientes a, sua corpora corruption; tradentes (a). Alios autem Origenianos continuo subjiciens:
passages.english: XLII. The Origenians were named after a certain Origen; not the one who is known to almost everyone, but some other, I do not know who. Epiphanius, speaking of him or of his followers, says: "The Origenians [are named] after a certain Origen; they are of shameful practice; these are the ones who do unspeakable things, handing over their own bodies to corruption." Then, immediately adding other Origenians:
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected: 'rere' read as 'fere' (almost), 'toquens' as 'loquens', 'corruption;' as 'corruptioni'. The stray marks '2', 'a' and '(a)' are footnote marks and have been left out. The passage breaks off at the colon introducing the next quotation.

passages.original: Cum Eusebii historiam scrutatos essem, cui Rufinus a se in latinam linguam translata subscquentium etiam temporum duos libros addidit, non inveni aliquam hæresim, qua:n non legerim apud istos, uisi quam in sexto libro ponit Eusebius, narrans eam exstitisse in Arabia. Itaque hos haereticos , quoniam nullum eorum ponit auctorem, Arabieos possumus nuncupare : qui dixirunt animas cum comporibus mori atque dissolvi, ct in ano sæculi utrumque resurgere. Sed hos disputatione Origenis praesentis et eus alloquentis, celerrime dicit fuisse correctos (Eu- stb , lib. 6, cap. 37). Jam nunc illæ commemorandæ sunt hæreses, quæ a nobis non apud istos repertæ sint, sed in recordationem nostrati quomodocumque venerunt.
passages.english: When I had searched through the history of Eusebius, to which Rufinus, after translating it into the Latin language, also added two books covering the times that followed, I found no heresy that I had not read of in these [writers], except the one which Eusebius sets down in the sixth book, relating that it arose in Arabia. And so, since he names no founder of theirs, we can call these heretics Arabians. They said that souls die and are dissolved together with bodies, and that both rise again at the end of the age. But he says that they were very quickly corrected by the disputation of Origen, who was present and addressed them (Eusebius, book 6, chapter 37). Now those heresies must be recorded which we did not find in these [writers], but which came to our recollection in one way or another.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'scrutatos' read as 'scrutatus', 'qua:n' as 'quam', 'uisi' as 'nisi', 'Arabieos' as 'Arabicos', 'dixirunt' as 'dixerunt', 'comporibus' as 'corporibus', 'ct in ano' as 'et in fine' (at the end), 'eus' as 'eos', 'nostrati' as 'nostram'. 'These [writers]' (istos) are presumably Epiphanius and Philaster, whose catalogues Augustine has been following.
